name: AI and Project-Based Learning
objectives: Given a project idea, list the essentials of a strong project and write a driving question that AI cannot simply answer, with a question that is local or personal and open

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Designing the project with AI

lessons.title: Lesson 1: PBL essentials and AI's place in them
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the essentials of a strong project and where AI helps or harms.
This lesson builds toward: Given a project idea, you will list the essentials of a strong project and write a driving question that AI cannot simply answer, with a question that is local or personal and open.
Strong projects share a few essentials: a driving question that is open and matters to students; sustained inquiry over time; authentic work connected to the real world; student voice and choice; critique and revision; and a public product shared with an audience beyond the teacher.
AI can help the teacher design all of this faster, and can help students brainstorm, research, draft and get feedback. It can also short-circuit inquiry: a student can ask AI for the answer to the driving question in seconds.
So design for it. The driving question should be local or personal enough that AI cannot simply answer it ("How can we reduce food waste in our cafeteria?" rather than "What causes food waste?"), and the learning should show in the process, not only the product.
Words to know:
- Project-based learning (PBL): learning by working over time on a real question and sharing a product with an audience.
- Driving question: the open question that guides a whole project.
- Authentic: connected to real people, places and problems.
Try it now: Ask an AI tool to answer a driving question you have used or seen. Then rewrite the question so it is local or personal enough that AI cannot simply answer it.
You can now name the essentials of strong PBL and design driving questions AI cannot short-circuit.

check.q: Which is one of the PBL essentials?
options: A worksheet graded only by the teacher
A single test at the end
A topic the teacher picks with no student choice
check.why: Strong projects include critique and revision, along with voice, choice and a public product.

check.q: Your driving question is "What causes air pollution?" How would you change it?
options: Make it local, such as "How can we cut idling cars outside our school?"
Ask AI to answer it first
check.why: A local or personal question keeps AI from simply answering it.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Driving questions, launches, milestones and rubrics
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use AI to draft the project's driving question, entry event, milestones and rubric.
This lesson builds toward: Given your grade, subject, standards and project length, you will use AI to draft an entry event, four to six milestones and a two-part rubric, checked against your standards and for a realistic timeline.
Give AI the grade, subject, standards (from your official source), length of the project, and your community context (in general terms). Ask for five driving-question options, then pick and refine one with students if you can.
Ask for an entry event that sparks curiosity (a guest, a mystery object, a local problem, a site visit) and for four to six milestones: research, plan, first draft or prototype, critique, revision, final product. Ask for the knowledge each milestone requires, so you can plan mini-lessons.
Ask for a rubric with two parts: the final product (content and quality) and process (collaboration, revision, use of evidence). Check that each rubric criterion matches your standards and that the timeline is realistic; AI often packs in too much.
Step by step:
- Give grade, subject, standards, length and context.
- Pick and refine a driving question.
- Draft the entry event and 4-6 milestones.
- List the knowledge each milestone needs.
- Draft a product and process rubric; check standards and timeline.
Words to know:
- Entry event: an activity that launches a project and sparks questions.
- Milestone: a checkpoint where part of the project is due.
- Critique: structured feedback on work in progress.
Try it now: Use AI to draft the driving question, entry event, milestones and a two-part rubric for a project you could teach. Adjust the timeline to fit your calendar.
You can now design a project's structure quickly with AI and check it against standards and time.

check.q: What two parts should a PBL rubric score?
options: The final product and the process
check.why: Scoring process (collaboration, revision, evidence) as well as product rewards the learning.

check.q: AI's project timeline fits eight milestones into two weeks. What would you do?
options: Keep it, since AI planned it
Remove the rubric to save time
Cut it to a realistic plan, such as four to six milestones
check.why: AI often packs in too much, so check that the timeline is realistic.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Research with AI: search, verify, cite
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Teach students a research routine that uses AI without trusting it blindly.
This lesson builds toward: When students research a project topic, you will teach the explore, find, verify and cite routine with a research log, so every fact used is checked against a real source.
In projects, students research. AI can help them understand a topic, generate questions and find search terms, but it can invent facts and sources. Teach a three-step routine: Explore with AI ("What questions should I ask about food waste in schools?" "What words should I search for?"); Find real sources (search engines, library databases, interviews, local data); Verify and cite (check every fact against at least one real source and cite that source, not the AI).
Primary sources are a PBL strength: students can interview cafeteria staff, survey classmates (anonymously), measure waste themselves. AI cannot do that for them, which keeps the inquiry real.
Have students keep a research log: question, source, what they learned, how they verified it.
Step by step:
- Explore: use AI to generate questions and search terms.
- Find real sources: search, databases, interviews, local data.
- Verify each fact against a real source.
- Cite the real source, not the AI.
- Keep a research log.
Words to know:
- Primary source: first-hand evidence, such as an interview, survey or measurement.
- Research log: a record of questions, sources, findings and checks.
Try it now: Write the research routine and a research log template for your project. Test it yourself on one research question from the project.
You can now teach students to research with AI while relying on real, verified sources.

check.q: What should students cite in their project?
check.why: The routine is to verify every fact against a real source and cite that source.

check.q: A team wants to know how much food their cafeteria throws away. What is the strongest step?
options: Copy a number from any website
Measure the waste themselves or interview cafeteria staff
check.why: Primary sources keep the inquiry real and AI cannot collect them for students.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Managing and assessing the project

lessons.title: Lesson 4: AI rules for each stage and a student AI log
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set an AI use level for each milestone and a log students keep.
This lesson builds toward: Given your project's milestones, you will set an AI use level for each milestone and give students an AI log template, with a reason students can understand for each level.
One AI rule for a whole project is too blunt. Set a level for each milestone, using your school's scale. For example: brainstorming, AI allowed for ideas; research, AI for questions and search terms only; first draft, no AI (students show their own thinking); critique, AI feedback allowed alongside peer feedback; final product, AI tools allowed for design and polish, with disclosure.
Students keep an AI log: date, tool, what they asked, what they used, and what they changed. It takes a minute per entry and makes AI use visible and honest.
Explain the reasons. Students follow rules they understand: "The first draft is no-AI because we need to see your thinking before anyone helps."
Step by step:
- List the milestones.
- Set an AI use level for each.
- Write the reason for each level.
- Give students an AI log template.
- Check logs at each milestone.
Words to know:
- AI log: a student's record of when and how they used AI.
- Disclosure: saying openly how AI was used.
Try it now: Write an AI use level and a one-line reason for each milestone of your project, and make a one-page AI log template for students.
You can now set clear, stage-by-stage AI rules for a project and make AI use visible.

check.q: What does a student AI log record?
options: Date, tool, what was asked, what was used and what was changed
check.why: The log makes AI use visible and honest, one short entry at a time.

check.q: A student asks why the first draft is no-AI. What would you say?
options: Because we need to see your thinking before anyone helps
check.why: Students follow rules they understand, so give the reason.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Checkpoints that show individual learning
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan checkpoints that show what each student learned in a team project.
This lesson builds toward: Given a team project, you will plan an individual checkpoint at each milestone, so every student can explain the team's work and their own part.
Team products can hide who learned what, and AI makes that easier. Add individual checkpoints at each milestone: a short exit ticket on the knowledge for that stage, a two-minute conference, a written reflection, or an individual explanation of one part of the team's work.
Use AI to help you prepare: questions for each checkpoint, conference prompts, and reflection questions ("What did you change after critique and why?"). Keep student names and grades out of unapproved tools when you record results.
Use team tools well: AI can help teams divide tasks, plan timelines and give feedback on drafts against the rubric. But every student should be able to explain the team's work and their own contribution.
Step by step:
- Add an individual checkpoint at each milestone.
- Use AI to draft checkpoint, conference and reflection questions.
- Record results in your gradebook or an approved tool.
- Let teams use AI for planning and draft feedback as allowed.
- Every student explains the work and their part.
Words to know:
- Checkpoint: a short individual check on learning during a project.
- Conference: a short one-to-one conversation between teacher and student about their work.
- Reflection: writing or talking about what you learned and how.
Try it now: Use AI to draft an individual checkpoint for each milestone (one exit-ticket question, one conference prompt or one reflection question).
You can now assess each student's learning inside a team project.

options: A two-minute conference with one student
A group grade for the whole project
check.why: Individual checkpoints show what each student learned, not just the team.

check.q: You record checkpoint results with AI's help. What would you do?
options: Paste student names and grades into any AI tool
Post results on the class website
Keep names and grades out of tools the district has not approved
check.why: Student names and grades stay out of unapproved tools.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: The public product, showcase and reflection
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan an authentic showcase with honest AI disclosure and student reflection.
This lesson builds toward: When the project ends, you will plan a public showcase with a real audience, an AI disclosure and a student reflection, following your school's rules for photos, names and online sharing.
A real audience raises the quality of work: families, community members, local experts, the school board or a business that faces the problem. Plan the showcase early and invite people with a short message (AI can draft it).
Ask teams to include an AI disclosure with their product ("We used AI to brainstorm design ideas and to check grammar; all research data was collected by us"). Honest disclosure is part of the product's integrity, and audiences respect it.
Protect students: follow your school's rules for photos, names and recordings, and for sharing work online. End with reflection: what students learned about the topic, about teamwork, and about when AI helped or got in the way.
Step by step:
- Choose a real audience and invite them early.
- Teams add an AI disclosure to their product.
- Follow school rules for photos, names and online sharing.
- Hold the showcase.
- Close with reflection on learning, teamwork and AI.
Words to know:
- Showcase: an event where students present their work to an audience.
- Authentic audience: real people who care about the work, beyond the teacher.
Try it now: Final task: assemble your PBL unit (driving question, entry event, milestones with AI levels, product and process rubric, individual checkpoints, student AI log, showcase plan). Share it with a colleague and revise one part based on their feedback.
You can now lead project-based learning where AI supports real inquiry and every student's learning shows.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Driving question and launch The question is closed or AI could answer it, or there is no entry event. An open, local or personal driving question and an entry event that sparks questions. Students helped choose or refine the question. Milestones and rubric Fewer than four milestones, or the rubric scores only the product. Four to six milestones on a realistic timeline and a rubric for product and process, matched to standards. Each milestone lists the knowledge it needs and a mini-lesson to teach it. AI levels and log One AI rule for the whole project, or no student AI log. Every milestone has an AI use level, and there is a student AI log template. Each level comes with a reason written for students. Individual checkpoints Only the team product is assessed. An individual checkpoint at each milestone. Checkpoints vary (exit ticket, conference, reflection) and fit each stage. Showcase plan No real audience, or no AI disclosure. A public showcase with a real audience, an AI disclosure and a reflection, following school rules. Names the specific audience and how they will be invited. Colleague feedback The plan was not shared with a colleague. A colleague checked the plan and one part was revised. Can say what changed and why it is better. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is an authentic audience for a project?
options: Local experts or families who care about the problem
check.why: Real people who care about the work raise its quality.

check.q: A family member at the showcase wants to post photos of students online. What would you check?
options: Nothing; it is a public event
Your school's rules for photos, names and online sharing
check.why: Protect students by following school rules on photos and sharing.
